item.title: 5 Reasons to Be Kinder When It's Hard
item.description:
Relationships

5 Reasons to Be Kinder When It's Hard

The real power of kindness shows up when people don't treat us that way.

Posted September 6, 2026

Key points
  • Kindness lowers the emotional temperature.
  • Kindness makes you stronger, not weaker.
  • Kindness helps you see the struggle behind the behavior.

We have all been through enough situations to show us that kindness is easy when people treat us well. But in this post, I want to talk about the real power of kindness, which shows up when others don't treat us so well. Of course, most of us see ourselves as kind. You notice it when your kids cooperate, your partner shows appreciation, your co-workers show respect, and even when strangers treat you well, it feels really good.

So, when the rubber meets the road, as the saying goes, is when others don't treat us very well. That is the real test because through my work as a psychologist with children, teens, adults, and families, I've seen just how quickly hurt can turn into defensiveness, criticism, retaliation, and withdrawal. That's why I encourage people to consider a deceptively simple idea: Be kinder when it is hard. Below, I'll explain five reasons why being kinder when it's hard is the better option more often than you may imagine.

1. Kindness Lowers the Emotional Temperature

When someone comes at us with anger, our nervous system prepares us to respond in kind, which can escalate the situation. The obvious problem is that escalation leads to more escalation, so calming down and problem-solving go out the window. Let me be clear: I'm not guaranteeing you that a kinder response will calm the other person down. But hopefully you'll agree that being kinder when it is hard keeps you from adding more fuel to the fire.

2. Kindness Makes You Stronger, Not Weaker

Couples therapists point out to clients, using the metaphor of a tree branch blowing in the wind, that flexibility is a sign of strength. If that tree branch snaps in the face of resistance to the wind, it is gone, but if it stays flexible, it stays attached to the tree. We sometimes confuse kindness with giving in, but they are very different.

The calm, firm, non-controlling approach I describe in my new book, 24 Hours To A Less Defiant Child, is about that: whether you are talking to a 6-year-old, a 12-year-old, or an adult child, compassion and boundaries can coexist. The more you lean into kindness with trust, the more you will see that it can have a backbone. That backbone that makes kindness have both compassion and strength exists in couples' relationships, friendships, and with co-workers as well.

3. Kindness Helps You See the Struggle Behind the Behavior

I have a sign in my office that reads, "Struggle With vs. Choose Not." An angry teen may be scared underneath their aggressive exterior. A struggling adult child blaming everyone else (Mom and Dad may have the exalted status of being top of the list) may be overwhelmed by underlying shame. What I mean is that kindness helps you understand what's underneath someone's behavior, and that doesn't mean excusing it. Rather, it helps you respond to the person, not just the provocation.

4. Kindness Protects You From Becoming Someone You Don't Want to Be

We all know what it's like to say things in anger that felt justified for about 30 seconds, and then wake up feeling terrible the next morning. And here's some good news: Being kinder when it's hard isn't only something you do for another person; it's also something you do for yourself. You get to leave a difficult interaction knowing that someone else's behavior didn't undermine yours. This beautiful quality of kindness, supporting our own grace and dignity when under pressure, is truly a gift that keeps on giving in our relationships.

5. Kindness May Mean Stepping Back

Stepping back, rather than immediately stepping in to help, is likely one of the most misunderstood forms of kindness. You may be familiar with some of my past posts on parents helping their struggling adult children. In these cases, they may repeatedly solve problems, provide money, make excuses, or absorb negative or even aggressive behaviors because, within someone they love, struggle can feel unbearable. Yet, in my books on this subject, I have shared that sometimes the more loving response is to communicate: I believe in you and care about you, and I'm going to let you handle this. That is not abandonment but rather making room for the adult child's growth.

article continues after advertisement

The Takeaway

Being kinder when it is hard doesn't mean tolerating mistreatment or abandoning healthy boundaries. It may mean listening more closely; it may mean apologizing; it may mean walking away when emotions are rising; or it may mean kindly saying no. As far as I can tell, though, if you value supporting your own grace, strength, and dignity, you can't go wrong with being kinder when it's hard.

item.title: What to Consider Before Homeschooling Your Child
item.description:
Education

What to Consider Before Homeschooling Your Child

What does the research suggest about homeschooling?

Posted September 6, 2026

Key points
  • Before making the decision to homeschool, you need to consider potential advantages and disadvantages.
  • Parents need to consider if they have the time, temperament, and training to adequately homeschool a child.
  • Success in homeschooling often depends on parents' time, temperament, and willingness to train.

In the aftermath of COVID-19 and the shutdown of in-person classes, there has been a rising number of children being homeschooled. What is contributing to that? For one, some parents are dissatisfied with the quality of public schools and the perceived quality of that education. Second, many parents are concerned about their children’s exposure to school-related problems, such as bullying, peer pressures, access to drugs, etc.

The research comparing traditional in-class education with homeschooling is mixed and there is no clear evidence that one is better than the other. Part of the problem is methodological because of who chooses homeschooling (for you research methods junkies, children are not randomly assigned to homeschool vs. traditional, so comparisons are difficult).

Let’s look first at the advantages and disadvantages of homeschooling versus traditional education, and then provide well-supported guidelines for parents considering homeschooling.

Advantages of Homeschooling

  • Reduced exposure to school-related problems (bullying, peer pressures, etc.).
  • Individualized instruction can meet a child’s particular needs that may not be addressed in school.
  • Flexibility of scheduling and accommodations for family issues, such as finances.
  • Family members get more involved in instruction. This is an important factor that has been shown to lead to better student academic achievement (regardless of whether the child is homeschooled or in traditional schooling).

Disadvantages of Homeschooling

  • Socialization with peers and development of social skills could be a problem (unless compensated for through outside activities with peers).
  • Parents have to cover a lot of subjects, so there may be unfamiliarity with some.
  • Parents could miss educational deficiencies that professional teachers and counselors would notice.

Critical Considerations If You Choose to Homeschool Your Child

Choosing to homeschool a child is a difficult decision to make. It has major implications for the child’s intellectual and social development and can have lifelong consequences. Parents should consider many things in making this important decision, but here are three research-based concerns for parents who choose to provide homeschool education.

These are the 3 “T’s”:

Time. Parents need to seriously consider if they have the time to devote to homeschooling. This includes time to research and prepare educational materials as well as the time for lessons and follow-up. This can be very difficult for working parents, who need to set aside enough time to do a thorough job of education, in addition to their other duties and obligations.

Temperament. Parents need to do a self-assessment to determine whether they have the appropriate temperament to be the child’s primary teacher (as well as a parent). Do you have the patience required? Will you be authoritative—enforcing rules but also supporting the student’s learning? Do you have the persistence to keep at it, despite fatigue and distractions? In the same way that not every individual has the temperament to be a teacher, not every parent will be able to adequately substitute for one.

Training. In addition to the proper temperament, homeschooling parents need to set aside the time to engage in ongoing training. Not every parent is going to be well-versed in all of the academic subjects your child needs to learn, so parents must be prepared to study and develop their own teaching skills. There is a lot to learn about effective homeschooling so parents must quickly become experts. It is important to note that homeschooling is legal in all 50 states, but that requirements, which include registration, subjects taught, testing, and documentation, vary by state. Do the necessary research and keep the required records.
